'''Eugenie Carol Scott''' (born October 24, 1945) is an American [[physical anthropology|physical anthropologist]] who has been active in opposing the teaching of [[young Earth creationism]] and [[intelligent design]] in schools. She coined the term "[[Gish gallop]]" to describe a fallacious rhetorical technique of overwhelming an interlocutor with as many individually weak arguments as possible, in order to prevent rebuttal of the whole argument.

From 1986 to 2014,<ref>{{cite web|title=Eugenie C. Scott: About|url=https://www.facebook.com/eugenie.c.scott/about?lst=100000604882571%3A544678527%3A1510861028|website=Facebook.com/eugenie.c.scott|publisher=Facebook|access-date=16 November 2017}}</ref> Scott served as the executive director of the [[National Center for Science Education]], a nonprofit science education organization supporting teaching of evolutionary science. Since 2013, Scott has been listed on their advisory council.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |title=Advisory Council |website=ncse.com |publisher=[[National Center for Science Education]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130810112828/https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |archive-date=2013-08-10 |access-date=2018-10-30|date=2008-07-15 }}</ref>

Scott serves on the Board of Trustees of [[Americans United for Separation of Church and State]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Who we are |url=https://www.au.org/who-we-are |website=au.org |publisher=Americans United for Separation of Church and State |access-date=14 June 2018}}</ref> Scott is a member of the Board of Advisers for the publication, ''[[Scientific American]]''. She is also a Fellow of the [[Committee for Skeptical Inquiry]] (CSI) and [[Gesellschaft zur wissenschaftlichen Untersuchung von Parawissenschaften|GWUP]].

==Early life and education==

Scott was born in 1945 in [[La Crosse, Wisconsin]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Knickelbine |first=Scott |date=1980-10-24 |title=Eugenie Scott |url=https://ffrf.org/publications/day/eugenie-scott/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website= |publisher=[[Freedom From Religion Foundation]] |language=en-US}}</ref> She grew up in [[Wisconsin]] and first became interested in anthropology after reading her sister's anthropology textbook.<ref name=inspiration>[http://www.spiked-online.com/index.php?/inspired/article/1903/ What inspired me to take up science?], Eugenie Scott</ref> She was raised in [[Christian Science]] but later joined a [[Congregational]] church.<ref name=":0" />

Scott received a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in 1967 and an [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in 1968 from the [[University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee]].<ref name=":1" /> She was an instructor in anthropology at [[California State College at Hayward]] from 1968 to 1970, then received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in anthropology from the [[University of Missouri]] in 1974.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=August 2005 |title=Eugenie C. Scott: Personal Data |url=https://ncse.ngo/files/pub/legal/hurst/20060110_Exhibit_4_scott_dec.pdf |access-date=12 February 2026 |publisher=[[National Center for Science Education]]}}</ref> She developed an interest in creationism in 1971 while a graduate student,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lam |first=Monica |date=February 7, 2003 |title=Berkeley scientist leads fight to stop teaching of creationism |url=https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/PROFILE-EUGENIE-SCOTT-Berkeley-scientist-2672260.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250817011018/https://www.sfgate.com/bayarea/article/PROFILE-EUGENIE-SCOTT-Berkeley-scientist-2672260.php |archive-date=2025-08-17 |access-date=2026-02-12 |work=[[SFGate]] |language=en}}</ref> and became fascinated with [[creation science]] literature.<ref>[http://ncse.com/rncse/23/1/my-favorite-pseudoscience My Favorite Pseudoscience], Eugenie Scott, from ''Skeptical Odysseys: Personal Accounts by the World's Leading Paranormal Inquirers''. [[Paul Kurtz]], ed. Amherst (NY): Prometheus Books, 2001, p 245-56.</ref> Her thesis at Missouri was titled, "Dental Evolution in Pre-Columbian Coastal Peru".<ref name=":0" />

==Career==

=== Academic ===
Scott's research work focused on [[medical anthropology]], and [[Skeleton|skeletal biology]]. In 1970, Scott became an [[associate professor]] of anthropology at [[Sonoma State College]]. She then left the college and worked as a teaching assistant in anthropology at the University of Missouri from 1971 to 1974.<ref name=":1" />

In 1974, Scott joined the faculty of the [[University of Kentucky]] as an assistant professor of anthropology.<ref name=":1" /> That same year, she attended a debate between her doctoral advisor, James Gavan, and biochemist creationist [[Duane Gish]] which piqued her interest in the [[creation–evolution controversy]]. She recalled that, after the debate, "we were greatly dismayed [...] The scientist talked science, and the creationist connected to the audience and told good jokes and was really personable. And presented a lot of really bad science".<ref name="NYT20130902">{{cite web |date=2013-09-02 |title=Standard-Bearer in Evolution Fight |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/09/03/science/eugenie-c-scott-fights-the-teaching-of-creationism-in-schools.html |access-date=2013-09-06 |work=The New York Times|last=Dean|first=Cornelia}}</ref> The event made her realize that creationism was "a movement that could have really serious consequences for science and science education".<ref name="NYT20130902" />

=== NCSE ===
In 1980, Scott worked to prevent creationism from being taught in the public schools of [[Lexington, Kentucky]]. Scott was appointed the executive director of the [[National Center for Science Education]] in 1987, the year in which requiring the teaching of [[creation science]] in American public schools was deemed illegal by the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] in ''[[Edwards v. Aguillard]]''. Scott announced that she would be retiring from this position by the end of 2013,<ref>{{cite web | url=http://ncse.com/news/2013/05/ncses-scott-to-retire-0014832 | title=NCSE's Scott to retire | work=National Center for Science Education | date=May 6, 2013 | access-date=2013-06-23 | author=Press Release}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2013/05/eugenie-scott-to-retire-from-us-.html | title=Eugenie Scott to Retire From U.S. Center That Fights Antievolution Forces | publisher=Science | date=May 6, 2013 | access-date=2013-06-23 | author=Mervis, Jeffrey | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624145901/http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2013/05/eugenie-scott-to-retire-from-us-.html | archive-date=June 24, 2013 | url-status=dead }}</ref> doing so on 6 January 2014. Her place was taken by [[Ann Reid]].<ref>
{{cite web
| url=http://ncse.com/news/2014/01/welcome-ann-reid-0015284
| title=Welcome, Ann Reid
| publisher=NCSE
| date=January 6, 2014
| access-date=2014-01-13}}</ref>

=== Worldview ===

Scott is a [[secular humanist]] and describes herself as a [[nontheist]]. In 2003, the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' reported that, "Scott describes herself as atheist but does not discount the importance of spirituality."<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2003/02/07/EB75914.DTL&hw=eugenie+Scott&sn=001&sc=1000 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216072504/http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2003/02/07/EB75914.DTL&hw=eugenie+Scott&sn=001&sc=1000 | url-status=dead | archive-date=December 16, 2008 | work=The San Francisco Chronicle | title=PROFILE / EUGENIE SCOTT / Berkeley scientist leads fight to stop teaching of creationism | first=Monica | last=Lam | date=2006-11-13}}</ref> In 2003, she was one of the signatories to the third [[humanist manifesto]], ''[[Humanism and Its Aspirations]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.americanhumanist.org/Humanism/Humanist_Manifesto_III/Notable_Signers |title=Notable Signers |publisher=American Humanist Association |work=Humanism and Its Aspirations |access-date=October 6, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121005105825/http://www.americanhumanist.org/Humanism/Humanist_Manifesto_III/Notable_Signers |archive-date=October 5, 2012 }}</ref>

=== Authorship ===

Scott is an expert on [[creationism]] and [[intelligent design]]. Her book ''Evolution vs. Creationism: An Introduction'' was published by Greenwood Press in 2004 and then in paperback by the [[University of California Press]] in 2005. [[Niles Eldredge]] wrote the foreword in the first edition. A second edition of the book was published in 2008 and in paperback in 2009. The foreword to this edition was written by [[John E. Jones III]], who was the presiding judge in the [[Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District|Kitzmiller v. Dover]] court case.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Scott |first1=Eugenie |title=Evolution Vs. Creationism: An Introduction |date=2009 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-26187-7 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Kitzmiller v. Dover: Intelligent Design on Trial |url=https://ncse.com/library-resource/kitzmiller-v-dover-intelligent-design-trial |website=ncse.com |publisher=National Center for Science Education, Inc |access-date=14 June 2018|date=2015-12-15 }}</ref>

She co-edited with [[Glenn Branch]] the 2006 anthology ''[[Not in Our Classrooms: Why Intelligent Design is Wrong for Our Schools]]''.

In 2006 Jon D. Miller, Scott and Shinji Okamoto had a brief article published in [[Science (journal)|''Science'']] entitled "Public Acceptance of Evolution", an analysis of polling on the acceptance of evolution from the last 20 years in the [[United States]] and compared to other countries.<ref>[http://ncse.com/news/2006/08/public-acceptance-evolution-science-00991 "Public Acceptance of Evolution" in Science], NCSE, August 15, 2006</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Miller | display-authors = etal  | year = 2006 | title = SCIENCE COMMUNICATION: Public Acceptance of Evolution | journal = Science | volume = 313 | issue = 5788| pages = 765–766 | doi = 10.1126/science.1126746 | pmid=16902112| s2cid = 152990938 | url = https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/eff0/3da0d3318b59857f3d443d497b87ef382d43.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200228145616/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/eff0/3da0d3318b59857f3d443d497b87ef382d43.pdf | url-status = dead | archive-date = 2020-02-28 }}</ref> [[Turkey]] had the lowest acceptance of evolution in the survey, with the United States having the next-lowest, though the authors saw a positive in the higher percentage of Americans who are unsure about evolution, and therefore "reachable" for evolution.<ref>{{cite web |author=Nick Matzke |author-link=Nick Matzke |title=Well, at least we beat Turkey |date=10 August 2006 |publisher=[[The Panda's Thumb (weblog)|The Panda's Thumb]] |url=http://www.pandasthumb.org/archives/2006/08/well_at_least_w.html |access-date=9 November 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060927164013/http://www.pandasthumb.org/archives/2006/08/well_at_least_w.html |archive-date=27 September 2006 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== ''Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District'' ===

In 2005, Scott and other NCSE staff served as scientific and educational consultants for the plaintiffs in the ''[[Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District]]'' case regarding the teaching of intelligent design in public schools. Judge [[John E. Jones III|John Jones]] ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. Scott said that "we won decisively" and "in triplicate", and "we had the better case."<ref name="PI" /> About the merits of the case, she said, "Within evolutionary biology, we argue about the details... and the mechanisms," but "we don't argue about whether living things descended with modification from common ancestors, which is what biological evolution is all about.... The Dover School Board wanted students to doubt whether evolution had taken place."<ref name="PI"/>

==Personal life==

Scott's husband, Thomas C. Sager, is a lawyer. They have one daughter and reside in [[Berkeley, California]].

Scott is a backyard [[beekeeper]] with two beehives, and is interested in [[colony collapse disorder]] and an advocate of amateur beekeeping.<ref name="SZ">{{cite web|last1=Richard|first1=Saunders|author-link=Richard Saunders (skeptic)|title=Skeptic Zone podcast #454|url=http://www.skepticzone.tv/|website=Skeptic Zone|access-date=28 July 2017|date=2 July 2017}}</ref>
